title: SIU clears Niagara officers in shooting death of man on New Year's Eve
subtitle: Police watchdog says man was in mental distress
article: The province's police watchdog has cleared two Niagara Regional Police Service officers after a man in mental distress was shot and killed outside his home on New Year's Eve.
Police were called to Rykert St. in St. Catharines around 4:45 p.m. on December 31, 2019 after reports of a man with a knife.

The SIU says that after the man refused to drop the knife, police officers discharged their guns and he was shot several times. The man, 56-year-old Fred "Troy" Penner, was transported to hospital where he died on New Year's Day.
Melissa Lane, whose partner is Penner's nephew, previously told CBC that he lived with mental illness.
In its report, the SIU says that a registered counsellor with the CMHA was at the call, but stayed in the police cruiser because the situation involved a knife.
The SIU also acknowledged in its report that Penner was in mental distress and said that police had visited the home a week earlier for a welfare check.

In its report, the SIU says that the first officer to come across Penner asked him several times to drop the large serrated kitchen knife he was holding. It also says she tried to talk to him by asking his name and saying that she was there to help.
Another officer joined her. But when Penner took a "few quick steps" toward the officers, the SIU says, he was met "with a flurry of shots" from the officers' guns.
The SIU says one officer fired five rounds and the other fired four rounds.
After Penner was shot, the officers put bandages on his neck to stem the bleeding and waited for the paramedics.
A video, shot by a witness, showed Penner on the ground with officers gathered around him.
The report says Penner was placed on an ambulance stretcher about 10 minutes after 'shots fired' was reported.
The director of the SIU Joseph Martino, says there are no reasonable grounds to believe that either officer committed a criminal offence.

He acknowledged that Penner was "possibly not in a position to respond rationally" to requests to drop the knife, but maintained that his actions left the officers "little doubt that he was not about to surrender peacefully."

In interviews with the SIU, police said that they had feared for their lives and fired their guns. Martino said he believes "their lives would have been in real jeopardy had they waited any longer to protect themselves."

The SIU says that while the officers considering using conducted energy weapons, they thought it wouldn't be appropriate because of Penner's heavy jacket and the possibility that they wouldn't deploy properly.
In hindsight, the SIU says, the officers might have agreed to split their roles.
The investigation interviewed 14 witnesses, including 11 civilians and three witness officers.
Lane previously told CBC Hamilton that Penner was a very kind man, a little bit of a character, and humble.
